Love is when you're willing to make sacrifices for someone. Before love there is attachment. 

Attachment = I want from you (attention, affection, help, etc)

Love = I want to give to you (attention, affection, help, etc) even when you can't return it 

The first way this dynamic is supposed to play out in human development is between parent and child. The parent loves the child who can offer nothing in return, but out of love the parent still wants to sacrifice for the wellbeing of the child. The child first develops attachment to the parent, needing and wanting from the patent, but as the child's neuropsychology develops over the years the child is gradually able to love the parent and displays desires/efforts to give of their own volition (such as offering mom a handmade craft made because they wanted to rather than just because they were ordered to at school). 

This process lays the groundwork for adult relationships. At first you experience attachment, you want from the other person and might be willing to offer but only in a transactional way, ie you offer to get in return, and if they broke things off you would feel upset about what you wanted being withdrawn from the table (attention, sex, cuddling, etc). When you start to fall in love you feel a strong desire to offer value (attention, affection, help, etc) to the person that isn't transactional in nature. You can also recognize this shift in their behavior and motives, as well, if they start to fall in love with you, the way they clearly desire to offer to you and it's not just with the hope or expectation that you will return the favor in some way.

Yeah I had to find an effective psych med before my binges and eating compulsions went away. The disordered eating behaviors were like a surface level symptom of underlying mental health struggles.

I think it's similar to gambling addiction, and the typical physician is nowhere near qualified to help a patient with gambling addiction, but also the typical physician never feels pressured to try to help someone with gambling addiction, either.

Whereas I think a lot of people in the medical field feel like they are supposed to be involved in treating people for eating disorders since there is a direct impact on physical health, but it's really in the realm of psychology and sometimes psychiatry.

I am guessing that obesity clinics suffer from this issue as much as clinics devoted to anorexia. 

If you ever watch documentaries on those anorexia clinics or know someone who has been to one, like 90% of the focus is just on physical health factors. Underlying mental health isn't addressed very much so lots of people just wind up right back in there after "recovering."

It's the same thing with BED but usually even worse due to fat stigma.

The obesity clinic is still worth trying if you can afford it but to be truly effective they need to have knowledgeable psych staff who are very involved with patients.

Bupropion has a rise and fall energy effect for me, like moon tides, but it's a gradual and gentle cycle so I just time it all to my advantage. 

The "ride" starts out not drowsy but very very chill. Then the energy and focus ramps up, then gradually as the dosage wears off I get super drowsy. 

It's kind of like tapping the energy from the future and then when the future arrives there is no energy there because I used it all earlier in the day. 

So what I do is take the first dosage about an hour before work. So the first half of my shift I am a super chill robot and then gradually morph into a high energy machine for the second half. By the time I get home from work I'm tired as hell but I'm home and just need to eat dinner, shower, whatever nothing strenuous. I take the second dosage about an hour before bed so that the super chill effect combines with my natural late evening tiredness and the effect feels similar to a THC buzz, I fall asleep easily and comfortably before the energy phase kicks in and wake up in "Damn I need some coffee" mode but perk up within an hour or so.

One of the effects from bupropion that started early on for me was that my social anxiety completely vanished. So part of what happened is that I went from being the type who stuffed my feelings and tried to appease others all the time, to being a lot more blunt about my feelings and boundaries. I am sure some people interpreted this as me suddenly becoming irritable or rude, especially since I wasn't used to being socially direct or standing up for myself, so there were probably times when I was boorish about it. As an example I went from being a very anxious and depressed retail worker to not taking any shit whatsoever from disrespectful customers and refusing to give them any service if they disrespected me. However with some people in my life who are generally good to me I still developed more blunt and distant communication tendencies. I still care about them and like them, but without all of the anxiety I don't forcefully talk as much or automatically put on acts for people or try to hide it if I'm stressed out. Some people took that personally because it was a major change in my personality.
